title: 1 · The engine in one pass — a trace becomes an action
summary: After this chapter you can take any fixture in `tests/traces`, run it through the C++ engine, and say which matcher fired, why, and where every field of the resulting Action row came from. We follow ONE real trace — `03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4`, 5 transactions, 5 leaf blocks, exactly 1 action — end to end: LZ4+msgpack fixture -> `Trace` -> `EventNode` tree -> `Block` spine -> the one matcher whose anchor opcode is present -> captures -> a 6-field build output -> an `Action` row. You also see the same matcher in its two committed forms, the `.mch` source a human writes and the compiled row the runtime actually executes, and you learn the one discipline that holds the whole port together: the C++ dump and the Python twin must be byte-identical. Everything here is deliberately shallow — each stage is one chapter later on, and this page is the map you hang them on.

sections.heading: Lab setup — three commands
sections.prose:
Keep a shell open at `S:/Dev/ton-indexer-clear/indexer` for the rest of the tutorial. Two paths never change, so export them once: the engine binary `…/cmake-build-debug-visual-studio/ton-mch-engine/ton-mch-engine.exe` and the IR artifact `…/ton-mch-engine/ir/mch_ir.json`. `-T` takes either a single `.lz4` or a directory (which it walks sorted, `.lz4` only).

The three commands you will use constantly:

1. `ton-mch-engine -T <fixture>` — no mode flag. Decodes the fixture and prints the transaction list plus the initialized block tree. This is the ONLY mode that spins up a TON actor scheduler; every `--…` mode returns from `main` before reaching it, single-threaded and deterministic, because their stdout is a compared artifact.
2. `ton-mch-engine --classify -I <ir> -T <fixture|dir>` — the whole match+build+merge pipeline, one `ACTION` line per produced block.
3. `ton-mch-engine --actions -I <ir> -T <fixture|dir>` — the same pipeline, but each produced block is serialized into a database `Action` row before printing.

Everything on stdout is byte-compared against a Python twin; anything advisory (orphan-node warnings, registry complaints) goes to stderr. When you pipe engine output anywhere, `2>/dev/null` is usually what you want.

sections.heading: The fixture, and why this one
sections.prose:
The corpus is 148 `.lz4` fixtures producing 199 actions. Most are jetton/DEX traces with 20+ transactions and several interacting matchers — bad for a first read. `03RZCW7mu3eJp-FWifVzKsRHafUrqQNu4E6YwZxvXJ0=.lz4` is the smallest trace in the corpus that still exercises a genuinely non-trivial matcher: 5 transactions, 5 leaf blocks, exactly one action, and the matcher that produces it (`vesting_send_message`) is a two-node chain with a real message-body parse and a fully declarative 6-field build. Nothing about it is a special case — no lookups, no host shapers, no post-processing, no merge of a composite into another composite — so every mechanism you see is the general one.

A `.lz4` fixture is LZ4-frame-compressed msgpack, written by the Python indexer's `recorder.py` and read by `tests/utils/trace_deserializer.py` on the Python side. It is a whole trace: transactions, their in/out messages, base64 message bodies, and a root `interfaces` section — the per-account interface data that `TestInterfaceRepository` serves. The C++ loader decodes only the fields structural matching needs and ignores unknown keys, so fixtures recorded by a newer recorder still load.

annotations.text: The trap in this struct: `opcode` is stored SIGNED, because msgpack carries Python's int and the indexer writes opcodes as int32. `0xA7733ACD` round-trips as a negative number here. Never compare `*msg->opcode` against a hex literal — use `opcode32()` at the bottom, which is the exact port of Python's `EventNode.get_opcode`.

A derived flag, not a decoded field: the fixture carries a `value_extra_currencies` map and the loader collapses it to "non-empty?". That is all any ported matcher asks, and keeping the map would mean owning a second value universe for no reader.

`content` is optional and its absence is NORMAL, not an error — a message whose body was not indexed simply has nothing to parse. Downstream that becomes a failed parse alternative rather than a fault; see [[parse-layer]].

The back-pointer is wired AFTER decode, mirroring Python's `Message.transaction`. It is why `Trace` must outlive everything built on it — a moved-from `Trace` dangles every `EventNode` and every `Block`.

sections.heading: EventNode tree, then the Block init spine
sections.prose:
Two structural steps happen before any matching, and both are straight ports of the Python substrate you already know: `to_tree` (from `blocks/utils/tree_utils.py`) links transactions into a message tree, and `init_block` (from `event_processing.py`) turns every node into exactly one leaf `Block` — `ton_transfer`, `call_contract`, or `tick_tock` — connected in the same shape.

Our fixture's tree, from the lab run above: the ext-in wallet tx becomes `call_contract 0xcfc2d330`, its child is `call_contract 0xa7733acd` (owner -> vesting request), and that node has two children — the outgoing `ton_transfer` the vesting contract forwards, and `call_contract 0xf7733acd`, the response callback. Five leaves, one root. The deep dive on ordering, merging and the deliberate deviations from Python lives in [[block-tree]].

excerpts.title: EventNode — the sentence that explains the whole tree

annotations.text: Read this comment twice. A node's `msg` is normally the INCOMING message, but a log/notification leaf (an outgoing message with no destination) gets its own node whose `msg` is that outgoing message. That is why an event-log opcode can be a matcher anchor at all — it is a first-class node, not a field of its parent.

`lt()` is the sort key for the entire spine (`next_blocks` is kept in min_lt-ascending order), so its fallback chain is load-bearing: tick-tock uses the transaction's lt, everything else prefers `created_lt` and only falls back to `tx_lt`. Get this wrong and blocks reorder, which changes which candidate a matcher meets first.
Raw pointers into `EventTree`'s arena — no ownership here. Python's GC hides this chain; in C++ the lifetime `Trace -> EventTree -> BlockArena` is what `TraceContext` (below) exists to keep intact.

excerpts.title: Block — one field with two lifetimes

annotations.text: `opcode` is set only on `call_contract` leaves. A block PRODUCED by a matcher carries no opcode — which is exactly why the anchor prefilter can treat the trace's opcode inventory as static while its btype inventory grows (see the matcher loop below).

The same `data` field is the leaf's constructor dict before matching and the build program's output after — Python's `Block.data` exactly. So `CAPTURE.data.x` in a spec means different things depending on whether the capture is a leaf or a composite; that is a property of the substrate, not a spec quirk. Values are [[value]].

A deliberate deviation from Python: the order invariant is maintained at construction and after every merge, instead of Python's sort-at-every-walk-site. Same observable semantics, but it means C++ code may read `next_blocks` raw — and it means a mutation that forgets to re-sort is a real bug class.
Iterative where Python recurses, because trace depth is attacker-influenced and the engine's rule is that no input may abort the process. Same rule shows up again in the parsers ([[parse-layer]]).

`TraceContext::root` is the block for the FIRST transaction (here `call_contract 0xcfc2d330`), not a synthetic root. The `root`-btype wrapper block you will see in `classify_trace` is created separately, per classification run — so "root scaffold" in a dump is an internal wrapper, never a second trace root.

An empty tree is an ERROR, not an empty result. Production turns that into a `malformed_trace` category rather than a silently action-less trace — the distinction matters for telemetry ([[prod-path]]).

sections.heading: The one matcher that fires — spec form
sections.prose:
Only one matcher in the artifact can possibly match this trace: the anchor prefilter keeps a matcher whose anchor is an opcode set only if one of its opcodes appears on the spine, and `0xA7733ACD` appears exactly once. Here is the whole matcher, in the form a human writes and commits.

Thirty lines, and every one of them shows up in the output you already saw. Two opcode constants, a two-node chain, a parse, and six output fields. The `--match` run below stops after the match phase, so you can see the captures before any building happens.

annotations.text: "The response is consumed … but only the request feeds the build" is the single most important invariant on this page. Matching a block does two independent things: it may bind a capture the build reads, AND it removes the block from the spine so no later matcher can claim it. The `response` capture exists purely for the second effect.

`opcode` declarations are spec-local names. Nothing downstream knows the identifier — the compiled artifact carries only the number, in decimal. Grepping `mch_ir.json` for `A7733ACD` finds nothing; grep `2809346765`.

`produces` names a Python Block CLASS, but the emitted btype is `vesting_send_message` — the frontend maps class -> btype through `indexer/events/mch/btypes.py`. The btype is what the serializer dispatches on, so that table is a real part of the contract, not a naming convenience.

The chain arrow walks the BLOCK tree's `next_blocks`, not the message tree. In this fixture `0xf7733acd` happens to be a direct child of the anchor, but the walker's reachability rules ([[matcher-runtime]]) are what actually decide, and they are not simply "is a child".

`send.msg.*` reads the message envelope and is available immediately; `send.body.*` is null until the `parse` statement on line 21 has run. Both are attribute accesses on the same capture, and nothing in the syntax marks the difference — the ordering of statements is the only thing that makes `body` non-null ([[parse-layer]], [[build-programs]]).

runs.note: Match phase only — no build, no merge. `block_key` is `btype#opcode@lt`, the identity used in every dump. Note `consumed` has two entries while the build reads only one: the response is claimed and removed from the spine regardless.

sections.heading: …and the same matcher, compiled
sections.prose:
`ir/mch_ir.json` is the committed compilation of every `.mch` file — one JSON document, 11.5k lines, produced by the Python frontend (`indexer/events/mch/`) and consumed by both engines. It has three top-level parts that matter here: `matchers` (one row per matcher), `nodes` (a FLAT array of match-tree nodes shared by all matchers and referenced by index), and `registration_order` (the priority order matchers run in). Our matcher is `matchers[32]`.

Read the row next to the spec above and the mapping is one-to-one. The point of showing both is that they are the same object: nothing is inferred at runtime, and if you ever wonder what the engine will actually do, this file — not the spec — is the answer. [[ir-artifact]] covers the format properly.

excerpts.title: matchers[32] — header, captures, first build statement

annotations.text: `2809346765` is `0xA7733ACD`. This set is also the runtime prefilter key: `classify_trace` collects the trace's opcode inventory once and skips a matcher's entire BFS when the intersection is empty. On this trace 32 of 33 matchers are skipped without ever touching a block.
`root` is an INDEX into the document-level `nodes` array, not an inline subtree. Match trees are pooled across all matchers, so node indices are global and a node can in principle be shared.

Captures are declared with cardinality (`one` vs a list form) and in spec order — and that order is their SLOT order. The generated build function addresses them positionally as `env.slots[0]`, never by name, so reordering captures in a spec silently changes the compiled program.

Both default to true: after a successful match the anchor's remaining excess/bounce children are auto-appended to the consumed set. That is the `auto=[]` field in the `--classify` line — empty here, because this trace has neither.

`build_program` is an ordered STATEMENT list, not an expression tree. `parse` is a statement with a side effect: it fills `slots[0].body`. That is why spec statement order is semantically significant, as flagged on the spec excerpt above.

excerpts.title: nodes[327] and nodes[328] — the chain, at the end of the file

annotations.text: Node 327 is the anchor: opcode + the capture it binds + a single `child`. `child` means "and then this must also match, somewhere reachable onward" — a chain link, not a tree branch. Branching kinds (`or`, exclusive-or, recursive) exist and appear elsewhere in this array.

`4151524045` = `0xF7733ACD`, capture `response`, no `child` — the chain terminates. This node has no consumer in the build program at all; its entire job is to exist so that the response block is consumed. Confirmed by the `--match` run: two blocks consumed, one capture read.

One `out` statement carries the whole field list, in spec order. Do NOT infer that order from a dump: the rendered `data={…}` is key-sorted, which is why `message_boc_str` prints first even though it is the fourth field here.

`send.msg.source` is three nested nodes — `attr(attr(name send, "msg"), "source")` — wrapped in a `call`. Expressions are trees of tagged JSON objects, and this shape is exactly what the code generator unrolls into a straight-line chain of `rt_access_build` calls (see the captured output below).

`fn` names a HOST builtin resolved by name. The set of legal names is not open — it is pinned by the registry surface dump that the Python twins consume, so a spec cannot invent a builtin that only one engine has ([[build-programs]], [[gates]]).

runs.note: A third representation of the same matcher: the build program is COMPILED to C++ at build time by `mch-codegen` (a CMake step), not interpreted. This file lives in the build tree and is not in git — which is why it is shown as captured output rather than an excerpt. Note `env.slots[0]` and the positional capture access, and that every step can `reject` the whole match. Full story in [[build-programs]].

sections.heading: Mode dispatch and the core/harness split
sections.prose:
`main.cpp` is a flat option parser followed by a chain of early returns. Every mode is a `run_*` free function that owns its own lifecycle; nothing is shared but the parsed `-I` / `-T` values and one startup check (`validate_registries()`, placed ahead of dispatch so even the self-test modes get it — see [[parse-layer]]).

Underneath, the code is split in two on a hard line. `ClassifyCore.{h,cpp}` is the PURE pipeline: `(TraceContext + LoadedIr + LookupSource + generated build table) -> a buffered per-trace result`, with no stdout, no filesystem, no fixture knowledge and no rendering. `Classify.cpp` is the harness that prints. That split is what lets the production actor reuse the identical pipeline ([[prod-path]]) and, more immediately, it is why a diff between `--classify` and `--classify-prod` can only come from the loader or the lookup source, never from the matching.

annotations.text: The `-schema` and `-prod` variants are not different pipelines: they run the SAME `ClassifyCore` with a different trace loader and a different lookup source. They exist to be A/B-diffed against the plain modes, which is how the production ingestion path is proven equivalent to the fixture path.

`--classify` and `--actions` are the same run; they diverge at one boolean deep inside the shared adapter (below). If the two dumps ever disagree about WHICH actions exist, the cause is the serializer's fill table, not the engine.

"no scheduler needed" repeats on every dump mode and is a real constraint, not a note: all of these return before the `td::actor::Scheduler` at the bottom of `main`. Single-threaded, deterministic, no actor context — required, because their stdout is compared byte-for-byte against Python.

"Trace-independent" is the whole point: matcher selection, the build-fn table, the lookup kinds and the anchor prefilters are computed ONCE per process. Anything you see recomputed per trace in the loop below is there because it genuinely depends on the trace.

The build table is a map from artifact matcher index to a plain function pointer, selected by the ARTIFACT's sha256. A mismatched artifact/binary pair cannot run silently — `prepare_classify` reports and the adapter exits 2.

No I/O in either signature. `prepare_classify` takes an already-loaded `LoadedIr`; `classify_trace` takes an already-loaded `TraceContext`. Reading files is the caller's job, which is exactly what makes both callable from an actor that gets its rows from Postgres instead.

`arena` is the CALLER's (`ctx.arena`): produced and proxy blocks are allocated into the same arena as the leaves, so the whole block graph shares one lifetime and pointers stay valid for as long as the caller holds the context.

A `CoreAction` is three block pointers, not data: `anchor` (where the matcher fired, used as the dump's identity), `produced` (the composite whose `data` holds the build output), and `aux` (the fire-time excess/bounce auto-append). Rendering — or building an `Action` row — happens strictly in the adapter.

"ATOMIC" and "NOTHING is emitted by the core" together: a mid-trace throw does not leave a half-emitted trace. The core buffers, sets `failure`, and hands the decision to the adapter — a dump prints `TRACE_FAIL`, production commits nothing. This is the C++ image of the Python classifier's per-trace try/except boundary.

The fallback mirrors Python's `try_classify_basic_actions`: on failure, reclassify with NO matchers and keep the surviving `ton_transfer` / `call_contract` / `contract_deploy` leaves. Note the honesty in the comment — no corpus trace fails, so this path is ungated, i.e. untested by the twins.

excerpts.title: The harness adapter — one function for both dumps

annotations.text: The contract of the whole dump surface in one comment, ending with the line that matters: the two modes differ ONLY in the per-action render. Any structural difference between `--classify` and `--actions` output is therefore a serializer fact, never a harness fact.

A preflight, not an assertion: a matcher referencing a message type nobody registered is warned about on stderr and build-skipped, so a half-wired protocol degrades into "this matcher never fires" instead of a crash ([[parse-layer]]).

`prepare_classify` runs once, before the fixture loop — and a table/fn mismatch exits 2 rather than running with a stale generated build table. That guard is what makes "rebuild the C++ after regenerating the IR" a hard failure instead of a mysterious diff.

`SKIP` lines are part of the compared stdout, sorted for stability: which matchers the engine refuses to run is itself a gate artifact. Our corpus run prints zero of them — every matcher in the committed artifact is runnable today.

sections.heading: The loop that actually runs it
sections.prose:
`classify_trace` is a port of the Python `event_processing` outer loop, and its shape is worth memorizing because every later chapter plugs into it: FOR EACH matcher in priority order, do a full BFS over the spine and try to build at every block. Not the other way around. That ordering is why the global matcher list order matters in the Python engine and matters identically here — an earlier matcher consumes blocks a later one would have wanted.

After every matcher has had its pass, host-side post-processing runs over a flat snapshot of the spine. Those passes are not expressible in the DSL (they merge across matcher results), so they stay hand-written on both sides.

annotations.text: One `try` around the ENTIRE matcher loop, and every result accumulates in a local `pending`. Nothing escapes on the failure path — this is the buffering promised by `ClassifyResult`, and it is the reason a spec bug can never produce a partially classified trace.

The prefilter short-circuit: with an opcode anchor and no matching opcode on the spine, the matcher's whole traversal is skipped. On our fixture this eliminates every matcher but one — and it is safe precisely because consumed blocks are never REMOVED from the inventory, so the set is a conservative superset.

`cur->parent == nullptr` is the consumed guard. A block absorbed into a composite gets a parent, so later BFS passes still walk it but never attempt a build on it. This one line is the C++ equivalent of Python's parent check and the reason double-classification cannot happen.

The subtle one: `next_blocks` is read AFTER `try_build` ran on `cur`, because a successful build MERGES blocks and mutates the tree mid-walk. Python gets this for free from generator resume order; here it is a deliberate statement ordering, and swapping the two lines would change which blocks the walk reaches.

btypes grow, opcodes do not. A matcher anchored on a btype like `jetton_transfer` can only match blocks a previous matcher produced, so produced btypes are folded back into the inventory after each matcher — otherwise the prefilter would wrongly skip every composing matcher.

The post-process passes see a FLAT snapshot of the spine taken after all matchers have run — not the tree, and not a per-matcher view. They are the ported Python host passes (`post_process_dedust_liquidity` and friends); [[actions]] covers what they do.

The filter that surprises people: a post-pass can REMOVE an already-produced action, and this is where that removal lands. "A matcher fired" is therefore not the same claim as "an action was emitted" — reconcile `--match` output against `--classify` output with that in mind.

excerpts.title: Per-fixture: framing, warnings, and the lookup seam

annotations.text: `=== <basename>` frames every fixture and the directory walk is sorted, so a whole-corpus dump is stable across filesystems. That stability is the precondition for diffing 199 action lines against Python with `diff` and expecting zero.
Orphan nodes are reported to STDERR, deliberately: stdout is the comparison channel and nothing advisory may ever land there. Worth internalizing before you add any printf to this file.

The lookup seam. For a fixture the interface repository is the trace's OWN `interfaces` map, decoded from the same `.lz4`; production injects a database-backed source through the same `LookupSource` interface. Our matcher performs no lookups at all, which is part of why it makes a clean first example.

sections.heading: From captures to an Action row
sections.prose:
`--classify` stops at the produced block. `--actions` takes one more step: `build_action` serializes that block into the wide `Action` schema the database actually stores — the C++ port of `block_tree_serializer.py`. The dispatch is a `btype` switch onto a `fill_*` function, exactly like the Python `match block.btype` you know.

This is where the fixed directional columns (`source`, `destination`, `destination_secondary`, `amount`, …) get filled and where anything left over goes into a per-type composite. Our matcher's six build fields split four/two. [[actions]] takes this apart properly.

excerpts.title: The one fork between the two dump modes

annotations.text: Here is the entire difference between `--classify` and `--actions`. Everything before this point — loading, prefiltering, matching, building, merging, post-processing — is bit-identical between the two.

A produced btype with no `fill_*` is silently skipped in `--actions` but still printed by `--classify`, so the two dumps can legitimately have different line counts. That is a coverage signal, not a bug: it tells you which btypes are matched but not yet serializable.

excerpts.title: The Action row is one wide fixed schema

annotations.text: One struct for every action type; unset fields are Null and render as `null`. This mirrors the Python `Action` model rather than improving on it, because the row has to line up column-for-column with what the Python classifier writes.
The standard directional quartet plus the asset quartet — the fields a consumer can read WITHOUT knowing the action type. Filling these correctly is most of what a `fill_*` function is for.

The per-type composites, one per protocol family. This list is the reason the project rule says to reuse an existing composite when the fields fit: each new name here is a DDL migration on the Python side too.

`accounts` is role-less on this branch — a flat set of participating accounts, one `action_accounts` row each. If you remember a `ROLE_SENDER`/`ROLE_RECEIVER` scheme from the Python docs, that belongs to a different era of the schema; do not look for it here.

excerpts.title: fill_vesting_send_message — six fields, four columns, one composite

annotations.text: Four of the spec's six output fields become standard columns: `sender`->source, `vesting`->destination, `message_destination`->destination_secondary, `message_value`->amount. Reading a `fill_*` backwards is the fastest way to answer "which spec field ends up in which column".

The other two go into the composite — and note the RENAME: the build field `message_boc_str` is stored as `message_boc`. Spec names and column names are NOT the same namespace, so grepping the DB column name in the specs directory will find nothing.

Compare against `fill_vesting_send_message` above — four columns plus the two-field composite, and note `message_boc_str` arriving as `message_boc`. `start_lt`/`end_lt`/`mc_seqno_end`/`tx_hashes` come from the produced block's event nodes, not from the spec.

sections.heading: diff-0 — the discipline behind every claim on this page
sections.prose:
The C++ engine is a PORT, and the thing that makes a port trustworthy is not tests of the port's own opinions — it is running the same artifact through the original and demanding identical bytes. `twins/py_classify.py` runs the real Python IR engine (the same `build_matchers` + `event_processing` outer loop) and prints the exact same line format. So the correctness statement for the entire pipeline is a `diff` returning nothing.

One fixture is shown below because it fits on the page; the real gate is the same command over the whole 148-fixture corpus, plus the same treatment for `--actions`, `--match`, `--parse-dump`, and the schema/prod loader variants. [[gates]] is the full story, including how to run all of them and what each one actually protects.

runs.cmd: diff <(ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I "$IR" -T "$F" 2>/dev/null) <(venv0/python.exe twins/py_classify.py "$IR" "$F" 2>/dev/null) && echo "OK: cpp == python, 0 diff lines"
runs.note: Both sides consume the SAME `mch_ir.json`. That is the point: the artifact is the shared contract, and a divergence is always in an engine's execution of it, never in two independent readings of a spec.

sections.heading: Check yourself
sections.prose:
Four things you can verify right now. If any of them surprises you, that is the chapter to read next.

1. **Know the corpus baseline.** The run below is the first thing to check after any change: 148 fixtures, 199 actions, and zero `SKIP` lines. Any page — including this one — that quotes different numbers is out of date.

2. **Prove the `response` capture is consumed but never read.** Read `specs/vesting.mch` line 19 next to the `--match` output above, then confirm in `mch_ir.json` that `nodes[328]` (line 11510) has no `child` and that `response` appears nowhere in `matchers[32]`'s `build_program`. A capture can be bound purely to remove a block from the spine — which is exactly why matcher ORDER changes results.

3. **Find your own anchor fixture.** Run `--classify` over `tests/traces`, pick any single-action line, take its `anchor=btype#opcode@lt`, convert the opcode to DECIMAL and grep it in `mch_ir.json` to find the matcher, then open the matching `.mch` in `indexer/indexer/events/mch/specs/`. You should be able to predict the `data={…}` keys from the spec's `out` block before you look at the dump. If you can, you have the loop.

4. **Test the claim that `--classify` and `--actions` are the same run.** Run both over the whole corpus and compare the `anchor=` values line by line. They may differ ONLY where a produced btype has no `fill_*` — the set you would get by listing the btypes absent from `build_action`'s dispatch in `src/ActionBuild.cpp` (around line 543). Any other difference means the harness is doing something the comment on `run_dump` claims it does not.

runs.cmd: ton-mch-engine.exe --classify -I <ir> -T tests/traces 2>/dev/null | grep -c "^ACTION "   # then the same with: grep -c "^=== "
runs.note: 199 actions over 148 fixtures, and the `--classify` run prints no `SKIP` lines at all — every matcher in the committed artifact is runnable against the committed build table.
